Eriocitrin Attenuates Diabetic Cardiomyopathy by Regulating Copper Homeostasis and Cuproptosis-Associated Pathways via SIRT7/YAP/ATP7A Signalling.
summary: Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a major complication of diabetes mellitus, with limited therapeutic strategies available. Cuproptosis, a novel form of copper-dependent cell death, has been implicated in cardiac dysfunction but remains unexplored in DCM. Here, we investigated the effects of Eriocitrin, a natural flavonoid, on DCM and examined the potential involvement of copper homeostasis, cuproptosis-associated molecular alterations and SIRT7/YAP/ATP7A signalling. Using high-fat diet and streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice, along with high-glucose-treated cardiomyocytes, we demonstrated that Eriocitrin improved cardiac function, attenuated myocardial remodelling and corrected glucose and lipid metabolism. Mechanistically, Eriocitrin improved myocardial copper homeostasis by enhancing ATP7A and ATP7B expression and reducing copper accumulation and cuproptosis-associated molecular alterations. Loss of SIRT7 impaired these effects, suggesting that SIRT7-associated YAP/ATP7A signalling contributes to Eriocitrin-mediated cardioprotection. The therapeutic efficacy of Eriocitrin showed similar protective trends to tetrathiomolybdate, a copper chelator. These findings suggest that Eriocitrin alleviates experimental DCM in association with improved myocardial copper homeostasis and attenuation of cuproptosis-associated molecular alterations, with SIRT7-associated YAP/ATP7A signalling potentially contributing to these effects.

Quantitative nanometer-resolution depth profiling of semiconductor implantation profiles using non-matrix-matched microdroplet calibration for LA-ICP-MS
summary: Laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) has gained increasing attention over recent decades, with continuous improvements in sensitivity, spatial resolution, and analysis speed. However, achieving accurate quantitative results remains a significant challenge, primarily due to matrix effects that influence the instrument response. The limited availability of certified reference materials (CRMs) for specialized sample types often necessitates either the use of non-matrix-matched calibration, potentially introducing considerable deviations even when internal standardization is applied, or the preparation of in-house standards designed to approximate the sample matrix. An alternative, less commonly applied approach avoids the use of solid calibration standards altogether by employing liquid standards. This strategy is enabled by specialized instrumental configurations that allow the introduction of liquid standards into the ICP while performing laser ablation under comparable conditions. In this study, we demonstrate this concept using microdroplets introduced into the ICP in an LA-ICP-MS setup. We systematically investigate suitable measurement and data acquisition strategies using a sequentially scanning quadrupole mass analyzer, combined with automated statistical data evaluation procedures. The performance of the method is validated through the analysis of Sr, Ba, Ag, In, Pb, and U in the glass reference material NIST SRM 612. Finally, the applicability of the approach to spatially resolved analysis is demonstrated in a high-resolution depth profile of an Al-implanted single-crystal SiC semiconductor. The results show excellent agreement with target values, representing the first application of this quantification strategy to spatially resolved measurements.

Simple sensitive ICP-MS method development and validation for quantitative evaluation and risk assessment of elemental impurities in anticoagulant drug product: study aligned with ICH Q3D guideline
summary: Abstract Background Elemental impurities in pharmaceutical products present significant risks to patient safety due to their potential toxicity. These impurities may arise from various sources, including raw materials used in the process, manufacturing operations, processing equipment, and packaging materials. In this study, a simple, sensitive, and reliable analytical method using Inductively Coupled Plasma–Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS) was developed and validated for the quantification of elemental impurities in anticoagulant drug products, specifically Apixaban, Edoxaban, and Rivaroxaban. The developed ICP-MS method enables accurate and precise determination of elemental impurities, ensuring effective monitoring and control of potentially toxic elements in these pharmaceutical formulations to support product quality and patient safety. The method targeted the determination of 24 elemental impurities classified according to the ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities, including Class-1 elements (As, Pb, Hg, and Cd), Class-2A elements (Ni, V, and Co), Class-2B elements (Pd, Ir, Os, Tl, Ru, Pt, Au, Se, Ag, and Rh), and Class-3 elements (Cu, Mo, Li, Sn, Sb, Cr, and Ba). The analytical procedure was developed using ICP-MS, and the optimised method was validated in accordance with USP General Chapter and , confirming its suitability for accurate and reliable multi-element analysis. Results The analytical procedure was validated by assessing specificity, accuracy, sensitivity, selectivity, precision, linearity, range, and LOD–LOQ precision in accordance with ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities and relevant pharmacopeial requirements. All 24 elements showed excellent linearity with correlation coefficients greater than 0.99. Accuracy was demonstrated across the range from LOQ (30%) to 200% of the target level, and recovery was within acceptable limits, i.e. 70%–150%, and the %RSD for precision was within acceptable limits, i.e. below 20%. Biofluid iodine concentrations are associated with mild cognitive impairment: The potential mediating role of thyroid hormones.
summary: Iodine nutritional status is associated with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) in older adults. However, evidence comparing iodine concentrations across multiple biofluids and evaluating the potential mediating role of thyroid function remains limited. This cross-sectional study was conducted in three regions of China with varying levels of iodine nutrition. Drinking water, urine, saliva and serum samples were collected from people aged ≥60, and the iodine concentrations in the water, urine, saliva and serum were determined using ICP-MS, and 24-h urinary iodine excretion (24 h-UIE) was calculated. Cognitive function was assessed using a combination of the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), the Activities of Daily Living (ADL) scale, and a structured questionnaire for cognitive-related medical history. Among 3888 participants, 1319 (33.9%) had MCI. Iodine status and cognitive outcomes differed markedly across regions. Higher levels of several biofluid iodine indicators were associated with lower MMSE scores. Among urinary measures, 24-h urinary iodine concentration (24 h-UIC) showed the strongest inverse association (β = -1.764, 95% CI: -1.973 to -1.555). Region-stratified analyses revealed substantial heterogeneity in iodine-cognition associations (all P for interaction <0.05). TSH was inversely associated with MMSE and partially mediated the associations of 24 h-UIE and 24 h-UIC with MCI, accounting for 10.23% (ACME OR = 1.012, 95% CI: 1.002-1.022) and 8.90% (ACME OR = 1.012, 95% CI: 1.001-1.024) of the total associations, respectively. These findings remained robust in sensitivity analyses. Our results indicate that in older adults, biofluid iodine concentrations are associated with MCI, and this association is only partially mediated by TSH.

title: De Novo Minibinder Radiotheranostics for Targeted Treatment of Prostate Cancer
summary: Project Summary/Abstract Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) is responsible for the vast majority (80-90%) of prostate cancer (PC) deaths and is characterized by rapid disease progression and limited treatment options. Since mCPRC develops in response to standard androgen deprivation and androgen receptor (AR) signaling inhibition treatment regimens, alternative therapeutic strategies beyond AR signaling modulation are required for mCRPC. PSMA-targeted Lutetium-177–PSMA-617 (Pluvicto) is the first approved radiotherapeutic for mCRPC, yet its effect is relatively modest (4 month OS increase) and most patients quickly progress, reportedly due to (1) PSMA expression heterogeneity, both within and across individual metastases as well as between patients, which results in suboptimal on-tumor radiation dose and ineligible patient groups, (2) dose-limiting systemic toxicities, and (3) cancer cell resistance mechanisms such as antigen loss (VISION Trial). While Pluvicto has clinically validated the radioligand approach in mCRPC treatment, next generation radiotheranostics can achieve more significant and durable patient responses by improving on-tumor radiation delivery, increasing coverage across heterogeneous tumors, and expanding biomarker-based targeting across PC disease stages and molecular phenotype. To this end, we have developed targeted de novo designed minibinder (Mb) proteins in small format (~7kDa) that bind diverse cancer targets with high affinity and specificity, can be efficiently radiolabeled, and can be engineered for tunable pharmacokinetics in vivo to maximize tumor accumulation while minimizing accumulation in radiation-sensitive normal tissues. Here we will apply our de novo Mb radioconjugate (MbRC) platform to target non-enzyme PC biomarkers B7-H3 and STEAP1, traditionally not targetable by small molecule ligands and peptides, which offers a promising approach for next-generation radiotheranostics in mCRPC. title: High‐Precision Rb Isotope Analysis by MC‐ICP‐MS Using Sr Empirical External Normalization
summary: ABSTRACT Rationale Stable rubidium (Rb) isotopes have received increasing attention as emerging geochemical tracers for investigating planetary evolution, water–silicate interactions, and global Rb cycling. High‐precision Rb isotope measurements by multicollector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (MC‐ICP‐MS) are commonly performed using the standard‐sample bracketing (SSB) method, but this approach is sensitive to short‐term instrumental drift. Methods Building upon the previously reported empirical external normalization (EEN) with 92 Zr/ 90 Zr combined with the SSB method, we adopted 88 Sr/ 86 Sr for EEN + SSB MC‐ICP‐MS Rb isotope measurement, owing to the closer mass discrimination between Sr and Rb. In this study, we correted the isobaric interference of 87 Sr on 87 Rb using an exponential law, compared Sr‐EEN with Zr‐EEN using the in‐house USTC‐Rb standard, and evaluated elemental doping effects (K, Ca, Na, and Mn). Results The results show that the USTC‐Rb standard yielded δ 87/85 Rb values of −0.15‰ ± 0.04‰ (2SD, n = 33) by Sr‐EEN and −0.16‰ ± 0.04‰ (2SD, n = 33) by Zr‐EEN, indistinguishable within analytical uncertainty. Elemental doping experiments suggest that the measured Rb isotope data were not significantly affected when the K/Rb, Ca/Rb, Na/Rb, and Mn/Rb ratios were up to 100. The long‐term intermediate reproducibility for NIST SRM 984 was 0.00‰ ± 0.04‰ (2SD, n = 121). Conclusions Because Sr can be effectively separated from Rb using Sr‐spec resin, this Sr‐EEN method provides a precise and reliable alternative for Rb isotope determination by MC‐ICP‐MS and exhibits high tolerance to matrix elements.

title: Roles Of Intermediate Filaments in Sensory and Motor Regeneration
summary: SUMMARY. Injuries to peripheral nerves frequently result in chronic pain, sensory loss, and muscle weakness. Even though regeneration does occur after peripheral injuries, its extent varies depending on the subset of sensory subtypes with best regeneration in motor and pain neurons and worst in proprioceptors. The differential ability of sensory subtypes to regenerate is not understood at a molecular and cellular level. Peripheral nerve injury leads to the expression of many Regeneration-Associated Genes (RAGs), likely necessary to mount a successful regenerative response. Data mining of sciatic nerve injury data bases revealed that different sensory subtypes upregulate different RAGs. Among them are some of the ten neuronally-expressed intermediate filaments (IFs). IF remodeling is thus a potential hallmark of nerve injury responses. The goal of this application is to test the hypothesis that the regeneration-associated (“RA”) IFs VIM and PRPH play roles in cell type-specific regenerative responses after sciatic nerve transection. IF proteins are mostly associated with forming elastic, deformable filaments that lend structural resilience. Neurofilaments (NF-L, NF-M, NF-H) are critical for maintaining axon diameter. There are several other neuronally-expressed IFs with poorly understood roles. Previously, we discovered that the IF nestin modulates signaling cascades. The IF VIM also plays signaling roles after sciatic nerve injuries: a soluble complex of VIM/importin/dynein transports pERK from the injury site retrogradely to the soma. In addition, several IFs are expressed in sensory subtype-specific ways, and two IFs (VIM and PRPH) are greatly upregulated after sciatic nerve injury. These findings form the premise that IFs are functionally important RAGs that underlie cell type-specific regenerative responses after sciatic nerve transection. title: Unlocking Natural Killer cell potential to combat breast cancer metastasis
summary: Project Summary/Abstract Metastatic disease is the leading cause of breast cancer-related deaths, with more than 42,000 patients predicted to die from breast cancer this year. This is particularly true for patients with an aggressive subtype of breast cancer known as Triple Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC), for which there are no targeted therapy options. Immunotherapies, which reengage the immune system to fight cancer cells, have shown limited and varied success in metastatic TNBC, and a deeper understanding of the anti-tumor immune response is essential to expand the scope of immunotherapy in this disease context. Though T cells have maintained a spotlight in immunotherapy, NK cells are the first responders to metastatic sites, and my data demonstrate a critical role for cytotoxic NK cells in controlling early metastatic outgrowth. However, tumor cells develop various mechanisms to evade NK cells, and a comprehensive understanding of NK-cancer cell crosstalk is lacking. To address this gap in knowledge, in my NCI-funded K00 postdoctoral work, I conducted a novel, in vivo CRISPR/Cas9 screen in NK cell-competent and -depleted models, and identified Phosphatidylinositol Transfer Protein Alpha (PITPα; gene name Pitpna) as a druggable target gene that promotes breast cancer metastasis in an NK cell-dependent manner. My preliminary data further show that Pitpna knockdown reduces early metastasis and promotes a shift in NK cell phenotype from regulatory to cytotoxic. This proposal will test the hypothesis that TNBC cells suppress cytotoxic NK cells through expression of PITPα, which can be targeted to restore NK cell responses and treat metastatic disease. I further hypothesize that gaining a more complete understanding of NK cell changes throughout the spectrum of tumor progression (from primary tumors to metastasis) will identify novel means to re-activate the anti-tumor effects of NK cells and treat metastatic disease. title: Sex-specific Mechanisms of Sympathetic Dysregulation in TMD and Comorbid Pain Disorders
summary: ABSTRACT Painful temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) are multifactorial health conditions associated with the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) and its muscles and nerves, and are considered one of a number of “chronic overlapping pain conditions” (COPCs) with a striking overrepresentation of females. These conditions arise from numerous etiological mechanisms triggered peripherally, centrally, or both, leading to sensitization involving inflammation, neuroimmune interactions, and nociplastic changes that maintain pain and dysfunction. A common mechanism that may underlie these processes at sites both systemic and local to the pain is dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system. Chronic stress results in over-activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the sympathetic nervous system (SNS), leading to a number of pathophysiological outcomes. The present study will test the hypothesis that distinct pathways of TMD etiology arise from disruptions in SNS homeostasis in a subset of people with painful TMD with or without multisite COPCs. In an observational cohort of TMD patients and demographically comparable TMD-free controls, we will determine the role of stress- triggered sympathetic activity in neuroplasticity, musculoskeletal coupling, and neuroinflammation. We will first assess the role of psychosocial stress in triggering the HPA-neuronal systems that lead sex-specifically to increased local nociception and pathological changes in TMJ musculoskeletal tissues. We will define sympathetic function/tone through proven approaches (heart rate variability, pupillometry, catecholamine and cortisol levels) and use machine learning and clustering analysis to identify a patient subgroup with SNS- mediated pathology (SNS-TMD group). title: Targeting C3 Activation in Aberrant Synaptic Pruning and Maladaptive Plasticity Following Pediatric TBI
summary: PROJECT SUMMARY / ABSTRACT Pediatric mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is a major public health concern, particularly when it occurs during early postnatal development—a period of rapid synaptic refinement that establishes long-term circuit organization and behavior. Repetitive mild TBI (rmTBI) during this window can result in lasting cognitive and behavioral abnormalities, yet the molecular and cellular mechanisms linking early injury to long-term outcomes remain poorly defined. Our preliminary work in a controlled mouse model of early postnatal rmTBI (postnatal day 14, PD14) shows that complement component 3 (C3) accumulates at microglia–neuron interfaces in the injured frontal cortex, coinciding with synaptic loss and persistent behavioral deficits. Pharmacological inhibition of C3 activation with CR2-Crry reduces pathological C3 deposition, preserves synaptic structure, and improves behavioral performance, suggesting that dysregulated C3 signaling drives maladaptive synaptic pruning and circuit dysfunction after pediatric brain injury. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that abnormal activation of C3 and its microglial receptor, complement receptor 3 (CR3), after early postnatal rmTBI triggers maladaptive microglial pruning of intact synapses, amplifies inflammation, and disrupts frontal cortical maturation, leading to persistent behavioral impairment. Aim 1 will define how abnormal C3 activation alters synaptic pruning and long- term behavioral outcomes, using CR2-Crry treatment combined with behavioral testing, electrophysiology, and high-resolution Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC) and electron microscopy. Aim 2 will determine how microglial CR3 signaling mediates aberrant synaptic phagocytosis and inflammatory spread using an inducible microglia- specific CR3 knockout line. title: Causes and mitigation of U–Pb fractionation during LA-ICP-MS analyses of zircon using nanosecond excimer laser systems
summary: This work investigates the causes of ablation bias in U–Pb dating of zircon by laser ablation inductively coupled mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) and possible methods for correction. Pb/U ablation bias occurs due to the relative volatility of Pb and changes with pulse count (pit depth). Measurements of NIST glass and zircon include significant ablation bias when scanned but since this is constant with time it is possible to determine variations in instrument bias by ablating under fixed conditions. Integrated signal profiles measured using laser pulses at 0.2 Hz combined with modelling of Pb/U fractionation suggest that the earliest Pb/U measurements (first 10 pulses) are affected by decreasing fractionation from a melt pool as it becomes increasingly depleted in Pb. This trend is opposed by deposition of depleted material as fallback, which dominates early signal loss. The fractionation sequence from the first 10 or so pulses is therefore chaotic. Ratios from the following 50 or so pulses show an approximately linear increase in fractionation. Normalized data from these pulses give trends with higher intercepts and lower slopes for standards with higher radiation damage during the same session. Fractionation and signal decay subsequently rise more slowly but remain linear, probably because fractionation is dominated by deposition in the deepening pit. An ablation fractionation model is proposed based on the drop in measured ZrO signal but this cannot be used to estimate accurate bias-free 206 Pb/ 238 U ratios because of the number of unconstrained parameters. The best approach for calibrating against an unknown is a direct comparison of all or part of the standard ratio profile with the sample profile after multiplication by a calibration factor. The factor that results in the best fit should represent a ratio of unbiased 206 Pb/ 238 U between standard and sample. Software is included to process and calibrate data. title: Epigenetic modulation of tumor vasculature to augment immunotherapy
summary: SUMMARY Tumor blood vessels allow anti-tumor immune cells to enter the tumor microenvironment, but abnormalities in the endothelium impair immune cell entry and responses to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). We found that genetic deletion of the epigenetic gene silencer DNA methyltransferase 1 (Dnmt1) in blood vessels primes the endothelium for cytokine stimulation, improving ICB responses. In our new work, targeting Dnmt1 in the endothelium in melanoma models with varying tumor mutation burden (TMB) results in notable regression of TMB high melanoma, increased CD4/CD8 memory T-cells, increased granzyme B+ effectors, and a reduction in lung-metastatic burden. In this R03 proposal, we aim to optimize and validate the use of vascular-tropic adenovirus to target Dnmt1 only in the lung microvasculature that could mitigate off-target effects of systemically delivered drugs targeting the epigenome. Our study aims to deepen our comprehension of how reprogramming tumor vasculature enhances anti-tumor immune responses, particularly when integrated with immunotherapy in the metastatic setting. Dr. Andrew Dudley, a Professor of Microbiology, Immunology, and Cancer Biology at UVA, leads the proposal. Dr. Dudley is the MPI on the T32 Cancer Biology Training Grant at UVA, a member of the UVA Comprehensive Cancer Center, and runs a research lab focused on tumor angiogenesis/tumor microenvironment. Dr. Craig Slingluff, a surgical oncologist with over 30 years of cancer immunology and immunotherapy experience at UVA, is also included. Dr. Slingluff’s research focuses on melanoma vaccine and combination immunotherapy development. A successful proposal will elucidate how vascular-directed therapies can augment the efficacy of immunotherapy against metastatic disease, pinpoint dose reduction strategies, and advance our comprehension of how aberrant tumor vasculature hinders anti-tumor immunity. summary: Project summary The goal of the proposed 5-year training and research plan for the Mentored Clinical Scientist Development Award is to support the transition of Dr. Liang-I Kang (PI) to an independent research career as a physician scientist. Dr. Kang has research background in liver biology and digestive system malignancies, with a focus on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). She is also a board-certified anatomic pathologist with subspecialty training in Hepatobiliary, Pancreatic, and Gastrointestinal Pathology. Dr. Kang’s long term goal is to lead an independently funded basic science and translational research program to study the tumor microenvironment (TME) in liver metastases. To achieve this goal, Dr. Kang proposes to gain new expertise in advanced tumor immunology and transcriptomics, through a combination of didactic training and a research project under the mentorship of Dr. David DeNardo, an expert on the TME in PDAC, and a committee of scientific advisors with expertise in pancreatic cancer, innate immunology, and genomics/bioinformatics. The research will be performed at Washington University School of Medicine, a leading institution in pancreatic cancer research, immunology, cancer genomics/transcriptomics, and physician scientist training. There is an unmet need for effective treatment strategies for metastatic PDAC, which has a 5-year survival rate of less than 5%. The liver is the most common solid organ site for PDAC metastasis and is associated with a worse prognosis. Better understanding of the liver TME may provide insight to candidate treatment targets. title: Human Chemo-Nociceptor Signaling
summary: PROJECT SUMMARY Chronic pain is an enormous and urgent health burden in the United States on a growth trajectory. Safe and effective alternative pain medicines to replace dangerous, ineffective, or addictive current treatments (such as opioids) have shown unsatisfactory clinical translation from animal models. We have developed methods to recover viable peripheral nervous system including the pain and itch signaling neurons from the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) from human cadaveric organ donors. These gifted, viable tissues provide unique opportunities to obtain high-validity human preclinical data on the physiologic, molecular, genetic, and cell signaling mechanisms that contribute to chronic pain. Recently, we showed that human nociceptors exhibit important genetic differences compared to rodent models that can impact clinical outcomes. In this project, we will leverage human donor tissue recovery to facilitate target identification, drug discovery, and the development of novel medicines to treat pain and itch. In Aim 1 we generate the first protein expression atlas of the human DRG at cellular resolution which will provide a comprehensive guide for drug targets. This highly multiplexed catalog of protein expression is possible with our innovative approach of imaging mass cytometry. The results will test the hypothesis that gene expression alone does not accurately predict protein expression, and we expect the proteomic data will challenge the current RNA-based characterization of sensory neuron subtypes. Next, in Aim 2 we investigate the physiology and intracellular signaling of the human chemo-sensitive nociceptors, focusing on the human-specific MRGPRX class of transmembrane receptors thought to be critical for pruriception, nociception, and inflammation. title: Formyl peptide receptor-mediated inflammation and pulmonary fibrosis
summary: Summary: Neutrophils participate in our immune defense through several mechanisms upon recognizing danger. One main neutrophil pattern recognition receptor, formyl peptide receptor 1 (FPR1), recognizes N- formyl methionine peptides derived from bacteria or damaged tissue. FPR1 engagement is one of the early signals required for recruitment of neutrophils to target tissue, and subsequent activation and inflammation. Although beneficial from a host-pathogen perspective, exaggerated neutrophil activation has been linked to inflammation and autoimmunity, including rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Though primarily a disease of the joints, extra-articular manifestations are common, with interstitial lung disease (ILD) occurring in up to 10% of the patients with RA. RA-ILD is a leading cause of death in patients with RA, with progression occurring even on current treatment strategies. Thus, there is a clear need to improve outcomes in patients with RA-ILD. The aim of the present study is to explore the role of FPR1 in the RA-ILD pathogenesis, with a focus on neutrophil activation. The premise is that N-formyl methionine peptides will engage FPR1 on neutrophils resulting in local inflammation and organ damage. To investigate this, we have two main aims. The first aim will characterize the N-formyl methionine peptides in RA-ILD using liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry of immunoprecipitated peptides from plasma and sputum of patients with RA (n=100), RA-ILD (n=50) and healthy controls (n=50). Peptides, either immunoprecipitated, or synthesized, will be validated for functional capacity using FPR1 cell reporter assays as well as in-house neutrophil activation assays in presence of FPR1 antagonist, Cyclosporin H. The second aim investigated the role of FPR1 in neutrophil-driven inflammation in vivo using the collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mouse model. title: Affinity-tunable Antibody Drug Conjugate (ADC) against High-Grade Serous Ovarian Cancer
summary: Project Summary/Abstract Platinum-resistant high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) remains one of the most lethal gynecologic malignancies, causing over 13,000 deaths annually in the United States. Once platinum resistance develops, standard therapies including liposomal doxorubicin, paclitaxel, topotecan, gemcitabine, PARP inhibitors, and bevacizumab achieve response rates below 15% and median progression-free survival of only 3- 4 months. Median overall survival in this setting remains approximately 12-16 months, underscoring the urgent need for new therapeutic strategies. The recent approval of mirvetuximab soravtansine (Elahere®) validated antibody drug conjugates (ADCs) as a therapeutic class in ovarian cancer, but its benefit is limited to the ~35% of patients with high folate receptor á (FRá) expression, leaving the majority of women without an ADC option. MUC16, also known clinically as CA-125, is expressed in more than 80% of HGSOC and plays central roles in tumor progression, metastasis, and immune evasion. Earlier MUC16-directed ADCs such as sofituzumab vedotin and DMUC4064A showed only modest clinical activity. Their development was hampered by three recurring barriers including interference from soluble antigen (antigen sink), restricted tumor penetration due to perivascular binding in mucin-rich stroma, and dose-limiting toxicities. No MUC16-targeted therapy has yet been approved. Mabswitch Inc. is developing a novel class of ligand-inducible ADCs designed to overcome these limitations. In the OFF state, these constructs circulate with attenuated affinity that reduces binding to soluble antigen and normal mesothelia, enabling broad biodistribution and deeper tumor penetration. title: Defect-Engineered LiYO 2 Interlayers Enabling Fast Interfacial Li + Transport in All-Solid-State Batteries.
summary: All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) are desirable for next-generation energy storage systems due to their high energy density and enhanced safety. However, chemical and electrochemical incompatibility between Ni-rich layered oxide cathodes and sulfide solid electrolytes, particularly Li 6 PS 5 Cl (LPSCl), limits practical applications. Direct contact between these components accelerates oxidative decomposition of LPSCl, forming resistive interphase products, sluggish interfacial Li + transport, and rapid capacity decay. Here, we propose defect-engineered LiYO 2 (LYO) coatings as chemically stable and conductive interlayers for Ni-rich cathodes. To improve the intrinsically limited Li + transport of LYO, aliovalent substitution is employed based on Li + defect chemistry. Zn 2+ -substituted LYO (LYZnO, Li 1.05 Y 0.95 Zn 0.05 O 2 ) and Zr 4+ -substituted LYO (LYZrO, Li 0.95 Y 0.95 Zr 0.05 O 2 ) are designed to introduce Li-excess and Li-vacancy defects, respectively. Importantly, both configurations successfully maintain the chemically robust Y-O polyhedral framework of LYO. When applied as nanoscale coatings on Ni-rich cathode particles, both LYZnO and LYZrO effectively suppress parasitic decomposition of LPSCl and improve Li + transport across the cathode-electrolyte interface. Li-vacancy-type LYZrO exhibits superior interfacial stabilization compared with Li-excess-type LYZnO, owing to more favorable vacancy-mediated Li + migration. These findings demonstrate that defect engineering of stable oxide coatings is an effective strategy to construct reliable and kinetically favorable cathode interfaces in ASSBs.

title: Development of laser ablation negative-ion ICP-MS for direct fluorine imaging
summary: The spatial mapping of fluorine in solid samples is heavily hindered by its high ionisation potential in conventional positive-ion ICP-MS. To overcome this limitation without using complex plasma modifiers or mass shift strategies, we introduce laser ablation negative-ion ICP-MS (LA nICP-MS) as a direct approach for fluorine imaging. We systematically optimised the critical instrumental variables governing dry aerosol transport and negative ion extraction, revealing that the 19F signal is strongly driven by the conditions in the extraction interface rather than the core plasma thermodynamics. Operating at a lower RF power (down to 850 W) cools the extraction zone and promotes electron attachment, while a deflector voltage between 10-12 V provides optimal focusing of the negative ion beam under dry plasma conditions. Using matrix-matched gelatine standards, the method demonstrated excellent linearity and a representative limit of detection (LOD) of 10.2 µg g-1. The analytical performance of the method enabled mapping of the fluorine distribution in a cross-section of a honeybee (Apis mellifera) exposed to a perfluorohexanesulfonic acid (PFHxS) diet, revealing clear fluorine localisation within the abdominal gut architecture. Furthermore, simultaneous detection of 35Cl and 32S demonstrates the potential of LA nICP-MS for the multi-element imaging of non-metals in biological tissue. Overall, this study establishes LA nICP-MS as a direct alternative for fluorine imaging and provides basis for extending negative-ion ICP-MS to other challenging non-metals in complex solid samples.

title: Elemental analysis of geological materials: A review of XRF, LIBS, ICP-OES, ICP-MS, and AAS
summary: Selecting an analytical technique for characterization of geologic material is a trade-off in sensitivity, elemental coverage, portability, and cost. This review discusses five important analytical techniques used in geochemistry: X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectrometry, laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), and atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS). Laboratory-based methods such as AAS remain the most accessible option for routine single-element analysis of metals and metalloids. ICP-OES enables multi-element analysis with high sample throughput and broad linear dynamic range that AAS cannot match. It offers higher sensitivity in the ppb to sub-ppb range, though it requires extensive sample preparation procedures (acid digestion). ICP-MS extends this sensitivity into the sub-ppt range and adds isotopic analysis. Portable XRF (pXRF) and LIBS (hLIBS) devices allow near-real-time on-site measurements with minimal sample preparation but have higher detection limits. Thus, no single method satisfies every analytical requirement. Important trends shaping the future of these techniques include the development of downhole LIBS probes, emerging hybrid instruments combining multiple detection principles, and machine learning methods that automate spectral deconvolution and analysis. This review highlights the analytical capabilities and limitations of each technique, with particular emphasis on detection limits, elemental coverage, sample preparation, cost, and portability. Thus, it provides a useful framework to select the most appropriate analytical technique for specific geochemical applications.

title: Investigating the Molecular Effects of Social Deprivation on Neuroblastoma Tumorigenesis and Progression
summary: ABSTRACT Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, with survival disparities disproportionately affecting socioeconomically disadvantaged patients. While socioeconomic status (SES) is a known predictor of poor outcomes, the biological mechanisms by which chronic SES stressors influence tumor progression remain undefined. This proposal aims to establish a mechanistic link between chronic socioeconomic stress, modeled through food insecurity, social isolation, and unpredictable chronic mild stress (UCMS), and neuroblastoma progression. Using immune-competent TH-MYCN transgenic and syngeneic Neuro2A tumor models, we will determine how SES stress alters tumor growth, immune suppression, and metabolic adaptation. Single-cell RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and metabolomics will define stress-induced transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming. Additionally, we will evaluate the therapeutic potential of targeting adrenergic and HPA axis signaling with propranolol and CRHR1 antagonists, alongside metabolic blockade with mTORC1 inhibitors, to reverse SES-driven tumor adaptation. These studies will provide the first comprehensive biological framework linking SES stress to tumor progression and therapy resistance, identifying actionable targets to mitigate disparities in pediatric oncology outcomes. This work will lay the foundation for integrating social determinants into precision oncology, ultimately improving survival for all children with neuroblastoma. Animal models are crucial for characterizing the effects of chronic stress on systemic tumorbiology, which traditional in vitro or clinical observational approaches cannot fully capture. These models enable controlled, longitudinal investigation of the mechanisms linking stress to neuroblastoma initiation, progression, and treatment response while accounting for complex, multi-organ interactions among neuroendocrine pathways, the immune system, and the tumor microenvironment. summary: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells are critical effectors in fighting against tumors. However, as cancer progresses, many of these cells are driven towards a state of functional exhaustion through chronic stimulation of their T cell receptor (TCR) by tumor antigen. title: Tunable Fabrication of 2D-Layered Magnesium Nanosilicates With Hemostatic Properties.
summary: Tunable fabrication of inorganic two-dimensional (2D) nanoclays is of substantial interest for fundamental studies and biomedical applications. Despite extensive work on inorganic biomaterials, layered silicate nanoclays remain a comparatively underexplored class of 2D systems. Here, we report an optimized hydrothermal method for the tunable fabrication of 2D layered magnesium nanosilicates (nSi). This approach yields disc-like nanoclays with lateral dimensions of ~20-50 nm and thickness of ~1-2 nm. The nanosilicates exhibit rapid cellular internalization, controlled therapeutic release in vitro, and the ability to form shear-thinning, thixotropic gels. Proteomic analyses indicate the formation of a protein corona enriched in factors associated with blood coagulation, consistent with in vitro clotting assays showing a concentration-dependent reduction in clotting time, with decreases of ~50% at higher doses. In an in vivo rat liver-laceration model, nanosilicate treatment reduced clotting time by ~75% and blood loss by ~45%, compared with controls. Collectively, these findings establish a tunable route for fabricating 2D-layered magnesium nanosilicates and suggest their potential utility in hemostasis and wound-management applications.

title: A novel approach for monitoring the spatial distribution and quantitative analysis of micronutrients in plant tissues using laser ablation ICP-MS imaging.
summary: Abstract Quantitative imaging of plant tissues by laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) is hindered by the lack of matrix-matched calibration standards. Established approaches, such as gelatine or homogenised tissue blocks, do not replicate plant matrices accurately. Here, we introduce a nano-dispenser-based calibration strategy that deposits nanolitre volumes of elemental standards directly onto paraffin-embedded grain sections, exploiting the low endogenous metal content of the endosperm to generate in situ calibration curves. Calibration performance for Mg, Mn, Cu, Zn, and Mo was assessed using LA-ICP-MS imaging and Iolite 4 data processing. The method demonstrated excellent linearity ( R 2 > 0.98), reproducibility across multiple grains, and sub-ppm limits of detection. Comparative analysis with in-house homogenised blocks and NIST wheat reference material confirmed superior accuracy and reproducibility of the nano-dispenser approach. As a proof-of-concept, we have applied the method for the quantitative imaging of metals in a whole barley grain section, and the results show excellent agreement with published data obtained by conventional liquid-mode ICP MS. The technique reported here provides a robust, scalable, solution for quantitative metallomics studies of plant tissues, enabling improved assessment of nutrient distribution and supporting the development of standardised protocols for LA-ICP-MS imaging.

title: Tracing Europe-Wide Copper and Bronze flow in the Dutch Late Neolithic to the Early Iron Age.
summary: The study of the production, movement, processing and consumption of copper and bronze objects in the European Bronze Age (c. 2500-800 BC) reveals the underlying mobility and interconnectedness of Bronze Age societies. Long-distance exchange networks spanned the European Continent, and this paper fills an important geographic gap in Bronze Age metal research improving our understanding of the metal flows across Europe. The Netherlands as maritime/riverine east-west and north-south crossroad is a key piece to the Bronze Age metal supply puzzle. More than 200 lead isotope and elemental analyses of copper and bronzes from the Netherlands, featuring the strategic use of portable laser ablation, constitute a key opportunity to test and reshape theories on Bronze Age metal flow. Our analyses indicate that the earliest copper is of Balkan and Slovakian origin with some import of Iberian arsenical alloys followed by an intensification of Slovakian/Únětice metal imports during the Early Bronze Age. In the early phase of the Middle Bronze Age, the Netherlands received fresh copper with nickel and arsenic impurities from both the Great Orme mine in Wales and Mitterberg in Austria, shifting towards Italian Alpine copper in the late Middle Bronze Age. Italian Alpine copper was widely used, probably reaching the British Isles via trade routes through the Netherlands. In the Late Bronze Age, high-impurity antimony-bearing copper sources prevailed in both the Netherlands and in Britain and highly leaded bronze became commonplace, with the added lead being consistent with British sources. The high-impurity element pattern can be linked to recycled Alpine metal with almost no visible contribution of Iberian metal arriving via Atlantic trade routes.

title: Alcohol Consumption, Blood Lead Levels and Aggressive Behaviour Among Adults Living Near Gold Mine Tailings in Gauteng, South Africa.
summary: Lead (Pb) is a neurotoxin linked to aggression, while alcohol consumption, a major public health concern in South Africa, may also increase aggressive behaviour. This study examined associations between blood Pb levels and aggression in adults, and whether alcohol modified this relationship. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 199 adults, living at varying distances from gold mine tailings in Gauteng. Blood Pb were log-transformed and examined in relation to environmental exposures (proximity to roads and mine tailings), behavioural factors (smoking, soil ingestion), and soil Pb levels. Alcohol consumption was categorised as none, 1-4 drinks and ≥ 5 drinks per occasion (heavy episodic drinking). Aggression was measured using the 29-item Buss Perry Aggression Questionnaire (BPAQ), including anger, hostility, verbal, and physical aggression. Linear regression models were estimated for each aggression outcome, adjusting for age, alcohol use, blood Pb, and interactions between blood Pb and alcohol. Mean blood Pb was 2.4 ± 1.8 µg/dL (range 0.5-12.2 µg/dL), with 9.7% exceeding 5 µg/dL and 18.7% exceeding 3.5 µg/dL. Higher blood Pb was associated with soil ingestion (β = 0.29, p = 0.017), higher soil Pb (β = 0.08, p = 0.001), tobacco use (β = 0.20, p = 0.031) and household dust (β = 0.13, p = 0.043). Heavy episodic drinking was associated with higher total BPAQ scores (β = 19.7, p < 0.001) and all subscales. Blood Pb showed marginal associations with verbal and physical aggression, and alcohol did not modify the Pb-aggression relationship. In this population, heavy episodic drinking, rather than Pb exposure, was the main factor linked to increased aggression. Addressing harmful alcohol use may provide an opportunity to reduce a modifiable risk factor for aggression, while environmental Pb surveillance and remediation remain important in communities with ongoing Pb exposure.

title: Water quality as an economic barrier to photocatalytic green hydrogen production.
summary: Photocatalytic water splitting has emerged as a promising technology for sustainable green hydrogen production because it directly converts solar energy into chemical energy under mild operating conditions. Although extensive research has focused on developing highly efficient photocatalysts, cocatalysts, and charge-transfer strategies, the influence of water quality on photocatalytic hydrogen production remains comparatively underexplored. In practical applications, hydrogen generation is expected to utilize a wide range of water resources, including freshwater, groundwater, seawater, municipal wastewater, industrial effluents, and reclaimed water, all of which contain dissolved inorganic ions, natural organic matter, microorganisms, and suspended solids that can adversely affect photocatalytic performance. These contaminants may adsorb onto catalyst surfaces, block active sites, alter surface chemistry, promote charge-carrier recombination, induce photocorrosion, and reduce long-term catalyst stability, ultimately decreasing hydrogen production efficiency. Furthermore, maintaining the high water quality required for stable operation often necessitates energy-intensive and costly pretreatment processes, making water purification an important but frequently overlooked contributor to the overall cost of green hydrogen production. This review critically examines the relationship between water quality and photocatalytic hydrogen evolution by discussing the effects of major inorganic ions, heavy metals, natural organic matter, salinity, and real water matrices on catalyst activity and durability. Finally, current challenges, research gaps, and future strategies-including contaminant-tolerant photocatalysts, self-cleaning catalyst surfaces, integrated water treatment-hydrogen production systems, and standardized testing protocols using realistic water sources-are highlighted to facilitate the practical deployment of photocatalytic hydrogen production. title: Synergistic Coupling of Thermal Decomposition-Ammonia Dissolution and Segmented Crystallization for High-Purity Ammonium Paratungstate.
summary: To address the escalating demand for ultra-high-purity tungsten in advanced applications such as semiconductor targets and nuclear-grade shielding, this study synergistically coupled the processes of thermal decomposition, ammonia dissolution, and segmented evaporation crystallization. The optimal parameters for the thermal decomposition and ammonia dissolution stages were subsequently identified through systematic optimization. By independently regulating the nucleation and crystal growth processes during the crystallization of ammonium paratungstate (APT), the limitation of traditional methods, which require multiple crystallization cycles to achieve high purity, is effectively overcome. Experimental results demonstrated that under optimized conditions-thermal decomposition at ~280 °C and ammonia dissolution at 90 °C-high-purity APT (4N5 grade, total impurities < 50 ppm) was achieved in a single crystallization cycle. Furthermore, under segmented crystallization conditions (nucleation at 80 °C with a stirring speed of 1.26 m/s and growth at 90 °C with a stirring speed of 1.09 m/s), the product exhibited an average particle size of 34.43 μm and a direct recovery efficiency of 73.1%. By suppressing burst nucleation and reducing impurity adsorption, this process provides a critical technological pathway for large-scale production of ultra-high-purity tungsten materials.

title: Application of a Zirconium-Titanium Phosphate-Phosphonate Composite Sorbent for Purification of Lithium-Rich Eluate Obtained by Direct Lithium Extraction Technology.
summary: Direct lithium extraction (DLE) represents an emerging technology with considerable potential for lithium recovery from low-grade brines. Nonetheless, DLE still faces several unresolved challenges, particularly concerning the purity of the resulting lithium eluates. The DLE eluate obtained in this study contained approximately 3600 mg/L Li, 2350 mg/L Ca and 1200 mg/L Na. Sorbent-based purification is regarded as one of the most efficient methods for eluate treatment. Among sorbents, titanium phosphates, zirconium phosphates, and zirconium aminotris (methylenephosphonates) are known for their high sorption capacities toward various metal ions. Therefore, this study aimed to develop a zirconium-titanium phosphate-phosphonate sorbent capable of removing impurities from DLE eluates. As a result, a novel powdered ZrTiPO 4 -ATMP sorbent was synthesized under mild conditions. Subsequently, a granular composite sorbent, ZrTiPO 4 -ATMP@PVDF, was prepared using PVDF as a binder. The obtained materials were characterized using XRD, FTIR, SEM-EDS, CHN analysis, and BET analysis. The sorption performance of the composite material was evaluated during the purification of eluates obtained from real oilfield brine. Under optimal conditions, calcium and magnesium removal efficiencies exceeded 95%, while sodium removal reached 60%. At the same time, lithium losses remained below 20%. These losses can be further minimized by returning the regeneration solution to the sorption step.

title: Rapid and Reversible Capture of PFOS from Complex Water Matrices by an Earth-Abundant Iron(III)-Carboxylate Metal-Organic Framework.
summary: Background Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) is a globally recognised persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic pollutant. Under China GB 5749-2022 and the US EPA 2024 drinking water MCL, permissible levels have fallen to 40 ng L -1 and 4 ng L -1 , respectively, placing unprecedented demands on remediation technologies. Methods An iron(III)-carboxylate metal-organic framework prepared from low-cost precursors (denoted MOF-LC, [Fe 3 O(BDC) 3 Cl]·x(solvent)) was synthesised via a one-pot solvothermal route from FeCl 3 ·6H 2 O and terephthalic acid (H 2 BDC). The material was characterised by PXRD, N 2 adsorption, FTIR, TGA, XPS, elemental analysis and ICP-OES. Adsorption performance was evaluated under varying initial concentrations, contact times, pH values, coexisting inorganic anions (Cl - , NO 3 - , SO 4 2- , HCO 3 - , PO 4 3- ) and humic acid backgrounds, and by a panel of six water matrices. PFOS removal efficiency fell from 99.2% to 85.8% over seven adsorption-regeneration cycles using a 1% NH 4 Cl/methanol eluent, with 90.6% of the initial BET surface area retained and Fe leaching below 45 µg L -1 . Conclusions Electrostatic, hydrophobic and pore confinement contributions are proposed as cooperative interpretations consistent with the observations. title: An Optimized Lipid Nanoparticle for Tumor Suppressor Restoration and Immunotherapy for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
summary: Summary Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) represents 90% of all head and neck cancers. Despite decades of research, the 5-year survival rate is 50%, and strikingly, the overall incidence rate is projected to increase by 30% in the next ten years, leading to far more cases, and unfortunately, far more deaths. One major barrier in the treatment of OSCC is the lack of novel therapies clinicians have at their disposal. A more rational strategy to develop safe and effective next-generation therapies is to examine the biology of OSCC. Two fundamental aspects of this cancer are that it progresses via the inactivation and mutation of tumor suppressor (TS) genes and has a severely immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). The major roadblock, however, is that LNPs have not been utilized to deliver small molecule drugs and mRNA in the oral cavity. LNPs must be optimized to the specific target area and disease, meaning there is no universal LNP formulation that can be substituted for OSCC treatment. summary: Uranyl ions (UO 2 2+ ) are hazardous to ecosystems and human health due to their toxicity, radiological risks, and persistence in aquatic systems. To detect UO 2 2+ in water with high selectivity, a unique nanocomposite chemosensor (UNS) was developed. A sustainable sensing platform was created by immobilizing 2-(((4-bromophenyl)imino)methyl)naphthalen-1-ol (HM) onto nanocellulose fibers from cotton linters. A simple one-step condensation of 1-hydroxy-2-naphthaldehyde and 4-bromoaniline produced the HM Schiff base ligand, which showed significant coordination affinity for uranyl ions. The UNS exhibited excellent analytical performance, with a rapid response time (90 s), an exceptional detection limit (3.26 ppb), and a linear range (0-0.25 µM), all below WHO limits. The sensor exhibited excellent selectivity for uranyl ions against competing metal ions in complex matrices. Its detection mechanism is based on chelation-mediated spectral shifts, represented as a hyperchromic shift in the UV-visible absorption spectra. The sensor was stable from pH 5.5 to 8.0, and the signal loss changed by less than 10% after regeneration for seven cycles. The use of CNCs as an environmentally friendly support matrix represents a co-benefit by tracking a major pollutant. DFT calculations indicated that uranyl coordination reduced the HOMO-LUMO energy gap from 6.003 to 5.39 eV, which accounted for the observed spectroscopic changes. Collectively, these results establish the UNS as a robust, low-cost, and field-deployable platform for on-site uranyl detection in environmental water monitoring.

The Role of Metals and Trace Elements in the Pathogenesis of Osteoarthritis and Other Rheumatic Diseases.
summary: Osteoarthritis (OA) and other rheumatic diseases are among the leading causes of chronic pain, disability, and reduced quality of life worldwide. Increasing evidence indicates that disturbances in metal homeostasis contribute to the pathogenesis of these disorders through their effects on oxidative stress, immune regulation, cartilage metabolism, bone remodeling, and extracellular matrix degradation. This review summarizes current knowledge regarding the role of essential metals and trace elements, including zinc, iron, copper, magnesium, selenium, and manganese, as well as toxic metals such as cadmium, lead, mercury, and arsenic, with primary emphasis on their involvement in the development and progression of osteoarthritis. Other rheumatic diseases are discussed briefly to provide a comparative perspective. Particular attention is given to the molecular mechanisms underlying metal-mediated pathology, including oxidative stress, ferroptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, activation of intracellular signaling pathways, and inflammasome activation. The diagnostic and therapeutic potential of metal-related biomarkers, metalomics, and targeted interventions aimed at restoring metal homeostasis are also discussed. Furthermore, current limitations of available studies and emerging research directions, including single-cell technologies, spatial transcriptomics, multi-omics approaches, and personalized medicine, are highlighted. A better understanding of metal homeostasis may improve the identification of novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets, ultimately contributing to more precise diagnosis and individualized treatment strategies for osteoarthritis and other rheumatic diseases.

title: Variable redox states of sulfur in porphyry copper-fertile arc magmas.
summary: Porphyry copper systems formed in magmatic arcs represent the largest concentrations of copper and most massive anomalies of sulfur worldwide. Whether the ore-fluid-source magmas were dominated by oxidized or reduced sulfur remains the subject of intense debate. Here, we quantitatively measured in situ the relative abundances of S 6+ , S 4+ , and S 2- in sulfur-bearing primary apatite grains hosted in zircon, amphibole, and biotite in igneous rocks related to porphyry and skarn copper-gold deposits in the Middle-Lower Yangtze River metallogenic belt, Eastern China. Calculated S 6+ /ΣS ratios of the sulfur-bearing apatite grains vary from 0.18 to 0.97 and are independent of the crystallization pressure and temperature of their host minerals. The data reveal two distinct groups of ore-fluid-source magmas: (i) highly oxidized, dominantly sulfate (anhydrite)-saturated and (ii) relatively reduced, dominantly sulfide-saturated. The results demonstrate that economic porphyry copper systems can form from intermediate-felsic magmas over a broad range of S 6+ /ΣS ratios and oxygen fugacities ( f O 2 ), possibly throughout Earth history including the Proterozoic and Archean.

title: Harnessing Cuproptosis Against Chemoresistant Ovarian Cancer
summary: ABSTRACT High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) remains the deadliest gynecologic malignancy, with most patients relapsing after initial response to platinum-based chemotherapy. Recurrent disease is almost uniformly drug­resistant, reflecting adaptive, non-genetic mechanisms that allow tumor cells to survive and regrow following treatment. Identifying and targeting such adaptive vulnerabilities is a critical unmet need. Recent discoveries from our laboratory have revealed a novel form of regulated cell death we teremed cuproptosis, which is triggered by copper overload in mitochondria. Cuproptosis selectively kills cells in a process regualted by FDX1 and resulting in copper targeting lipoylated and Fe-S cluster proteins, leading to catastrophic proteotoxic stress. Preliminary data from our patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models show that HGSOC cells exhibit enhanced sensitivity to cuproptosis, particularly when cultured in ascites-derived media that mimic the tumor microenvironment. Notably, the copper ionophore elesclomol (ES), previously tested in cancer clinical trials without mechanistic guidance, emerges as a potent cuproptosis inducer in FDX1 + HGSOC models. We have further developed a new analog, ESCU002, with improved solubility, pharmacokinetics, and in vivo efficacy. Animal models are required because drug exposure, copper delivery, tumor growth, ascites-associated microenvironmental effects, and platinum response cannot be fully modeled in vitro. Orthotopic HGSOC PDX models allow us to test pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamic target engagement, and antitumor efficacy in a clinically relevant and physiological settings. This R21 proposal tests the hypothesis that FDX1 + HGSOC cells are intrinsically sensitive to cuproptosis and that inducing this pathway can suppress tumor progression and prevent the emergence of platinum resistance. title: Macrophages in Intraocular Pressure Homeostasis and Glaucoma
summary: ABSTRACT Intraocular pressure (IOP), the primary risk factor for glaucoma, is typically tightly regulated in healthy eyes by the conventional outflow tract. However, approximately 10% of individuals develop ocular hypertension which places them at elevated risk for glaucoma, the leading cause of irreversible vision loss worldwide. The immune system appears to play an important role in glaucoma, as suggested by macrophage-related gene sets identified in genome-wide association studies; existing glaucoma therapies such as prostaglandin analogs and laser trabeculoplasty that induce an immune response; and immune modulators like glucocorticoids that alter IOP homeostasis. Yet, the functions and underlying mechanistic roles of the immune system in ocular hypertension are poorly understood. Macrophages are mononuclear phagocytic immune cells that are defined by their developmental origin as prenatally derived or adult/bone marrow derived. Prenatally derived, or long- lived macrophages, reside in many tissues in the body, and these resident tissue macrophages (RTMs) take on microenvironment-specific functions to maintain tissue homeostasis. My K08 work demonstrated that RTMs are enriched in trabecular meshwork, the main resistance generating tissue in the conventional outflow tract. Moreover, we demonstrated trabecular meshwork RTMs play a central role in IOP homeostasis, as their depletion resulted in extracellular matrix (ECM) turnover defects, culminating in increased IOP due to impaired outflow facility. However, the precise mechanisms by which RTMs maintain IOP homeostasis and whether their pro-homeostatic roles support resilience in ocular hypertension settings is completely unknown, highlighting an unmet need to understand the role of macrophages in IOP dysfunction and ECM dysregulation in glaucoma pathogenesis. To address this gap in knowledge, our Aim 1 is designed to profile genetically traced RTMs in trabecular meshwork by single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq)

title: Dissolution Behavior of Mineral Elements in Dahongpao Tea, Its Association with Flavor Quality, and Potential Contribution of Infusions to Dietary Reference Intakes.
summary: Mineral elements affect tea nutritional and flavor quality, but systematic research on their dissolution behavior and links to volatile and taste profiles in Dahongpao tea is lacking, as is evidence regarding contribution to mineral intake for different populations. In this study, nine Dahongpao teas were brewed five times. Eleven elements were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) with first-order kinetic fitting; volatile profiles were analyzed by electronic nose and taste attributes by electronic tongue; the contribution of tea infusions to dietary reference intakes was estimated from Chinese Dietary Reference Intakes (2023). The results showed that electronic nose analysis revealed distinct variation in volatile compound classes among the nine samples, with broad range and sulfur-organic compounds showing the highest response intensities. Electronic tongue analysis showed clear differences in taste profiles, particularly in astringency, umami, and sweetness, across the nine samples. Regarding dissolution behavior, Mg had the highest dissolution rate (67.24-70.94%), while Fe, Ca, K, and Zn were below 10%; dissolution followed first-order kinetics and total dissolved amounts correlated with total contents except for Fe. Network analysis integrating element data with volatile and taste profiles demonstrated that Mg and Mo contents were positively correlated with multiple volatile classes (e.g., sulfur-organic, broad range), while Ca, Mg, and Fe dissolution rates significantly correlated with richness and aftertaste-A, and Mo inversely correlated with sourness and saltiness. Contribution assessment showed that only Ca, K, Mg, and Se could be marginally supplemented, but the tea amounts needed far exceeded typical intake. In summary, element dissolution in Dahongpao tea is co-regulated by brew count and total content, with complex element-flavor interactions. title: Mineralogical and geochemical provenance reference for turquoise from the Teghout Cu-Mo deposit in Armenia.
summary: Turquoise from the Teghout Cu-Mo porphyry deposit (Lori Province, northern Armenia) forms veinlets and nodules in the supergene zone with quartz, Fe-Mn oxides, jarosite, barite and clay minerals, locally chalcanthite and gypsum. We provide the first integrated reference dataset for a substantial Caucasus turquoise source, providing the mineralogical and geochemical reference data needed to support future archaeological provenance research, collection authentication and heritage-science studies of exchange in the region. We emphasise that the Teghout occurrence was only discovered in 1974 during modern exploration and that no archaeological evidence currently links it to ancient turquoise supply; the reference framework presented here is intended to enable, not to substitute for, such future archaeological investigation. Gemmological testing, SEM imaging, EPMA, FTIR, Raman and LA-ICP-MS define a Cu-Al dominant turquoise near the ideal end-member. Raman spectra include variants with sulphate bands near 983 and 1007 cm -1 . Trace elements show MREE-peaked, chondrite-normalised REE patterns with a broad Sm-Gd maximum, weak Eu anomalies, enrichment in Sr-Mo-Zn-Sc and very low V-Cr. Comparison with datasets from Meiduk (Iran) and Tongling (China), two porphyry-hosted turquoise localities, tests discrimination within a shared genetic framework; log-transformed Sr/V-Pb/Ba and Sr/U-Pb/U ratios distinguish the deposits statistically, although the Sr/U-Pb/U field is treated as supportive because Teghout and Meiduk show limited envelope overlap.

title: A Subcellular Keap1-Nrf2 Disruption Strategy for Atopic Dermatitis Therapy.
summary: Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) is a promising target for atopic dermatitis due to its role in skin barrier repair, yet effective modulators of Nrf2 are lacking. Here, we report an itaconate-iridium(III) complex conjugation strategy for the disruption of the Keap1-Nrf2 protein-protein interaction (PPI) for treating atopic dermatitis. The conjugate (1) specifically engages cytoplasmic Keap1 to restore Nrf2 activity, thus upregulating anti-inflammatory genes HO-1 and NQO1 while suppressing reactive oxygen species (ROS) in keratinocytes. It also reduces IL-13 production and boosts skin barrier proteins filaggrin and involucrin in a reconstructed human epidermis (RHE) model. In vivo studies revealed that compound 1 ameliorated DNFB-induced atopic dermatitis-like lesions and hypersensitivity. Its optical characteristics further enabled the flow cytometric discrimination of HaCaT cells based on Keap1 levels. This work provides a promising strategy for developing bioactive molecules to efficiently disrupt subcellular PPIs, laying the basis to progress theranostic candidates for atopic dermatitis.

title: Anti-PD1 driven tissue pathogenesis, towards preventing and treating irAE toxicity during cancer therapy
summary: Project Summary Immunotherapy, the new fourth arm of cancer care is routinely used alongside surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. Immunotherapy has transformed patient outcomes for melanoma skin cancer and is being tested in 29 other cancers. Within immunotherapy, immune checkpoint blockade is most widely used, drugs unleashing T cells to expand their activity. However, in most patients, immune checkpoint blockade such as anti-PD1 unleashes the immune response against not only tumor, but also a patient's peripheral tissues (such as skin, gut and lung). These tissue off-target side effects are known as immune related adverse events (irAE). Tissue toxicities limit cancer therapy use both alone, or in combination, and can cause death. This application proposes to perform patient-centered clinical investigation and advanced ‘omics pipelines with human specimens. This proposal leverages a multidisciplinary approach spanning human and mouse tissue and tumor immunology. The investigative team will apply new foundation immunologic insights in PD-1 biology and immune memory to new pre-clinical mouse models to understand the in vivo mechanisms driving these toxicity events and to test interventions. Pre-clinical animal models are needed to test pathophysiology and intervention and systemic immune responses leading to tissue toxicity as related to cancer outcomes, which cannot be performed in humans. Together, this allows a detailed interrogation of intervenable tissue toxicity mechanisms and pathophysiology, and anti-tumoral immunity simultaneously, with the potential to improve cancer care.

title: Defining host and Clostridioides difficile responses to metal and oxidative stress during inflammation.
summary: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT All domains of life require nutrient metals, such as manganese, for fundamental life processes, therefore immune-dependent metal depletion can prevent the growth of microbial pathogens in a process called nutritional immunity. Clostridioides difficile is a microbial pathogen of the gastrointestinal tract and a leading cause of hospital-acquired diarrhea. Nutritional immunity is particularly important during C. difficile infection which leads to massive inflammation and immune-mediated metal limitation. Calprotectin is an abundant immune protein that sequesters nutrient metals and alters the transcription of C. difficile, but its impact on host gene expression remains unclear. In addition to metal limitation, the obligate anaerobe C. difficile must overcome exposure to oxidative stress, particularly during gut inflammation when oxygen levels increase. To sense and respond to these stressors, C. difficile possesses regulatory mechanisms that increase the expression of both metal transporters and enzymes that detoxify reactive oxygen species. Preliminary data suggest that inactivation of the C. difficile protein CD196_RS17790 increases the fitness of C. difficile in metal deplete conditions by maintaining manganese homeostasis. Manganese has redox potential and is a cofactor of C. difficile enzymes that prevent oxidative damage, leading to the hypothesis that CD196_RS17790 contributes to the ability of C. difficile to resist nutritional immunity and oxidative stress. A strain of C. difficile with CD196_RS17790 inactivated (Δ17790) has been created and will be used to functionally and biochemically characterize CD196_RS17790 in Aim 1. The growth of wildtype and Δ17790 C. difficile will be assessed in metal-limited and -excess conditions as well as in the presence of H2O2. title: Development of EDI-239382, a novel IRAK4 inhibitor to control inflammation driven metastasis, immune dysfunction and chemoresistance niche in ovarian tumors.
summary: ABSTRACT Epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) is an aggressive and life-threatening gynecologic malignancy. Despite decades of research, the 5-year survival rate for EOC patients remains dismally poor, with current therapies reaching a plateau. The biggest challenge lies in preventing or reducing recurrent disease, as existing treatments provide limited benefits relative to their toxicity. We are investigating the role of IL-1/IRAK4 (Interleukin-1 Receptor-Associated Kinase 4) in cell adhesion, metastasis, tumor growth, and chemoresistance in EOC. To address these mechanisms, we have conducted multiple medicinal chemistry campaigns, leading to the development of novel and selective IRAK4 inhibitors. One such inhibitor, UR241-2, was licensed by Empire Discovery Institute Therapeutics (EDIT). Through focused efforts we have identified an improved analog EDI-238382, which exhibits superior murine microsomal stability compared to UR241-2. In this proposal, we aim to advance EDI-238382, a novel, highly potent, and orally active IRAK1/4 inhibitor, to target TLR/IL1-driven cell adhesion, metastasis, chemoresistance, immune evasion, and tumor growth in a high-grade serous EOC model that recapitulates the recently recognized fallopian tube origin of the disease. Aim 1: Evaluate the absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) profile of EDI-238382. Aim 2: Determine the antitumor efficacy of EDI-238382 in a murine syngeneic EOC model and assess the therapeutic benefits of combining EDI-238382 with rapamycin and paclitaxel. This study is innovative as it seeks to develop an orally active IRAK1/4 inhibitor (EDI-238382) to improve EOC treatment, particularly addressing recurrence when tumor cells predominantly adhere to peritoneal walls after omentum removal. The overall significance of this research lies in its potential to enhance survival outcomes for the more than 22,580 patients diagnosed with EOC annually in the USA alone.

title: Dissolution-redeposition dynamics as a universal restructuring mechanism of electrocatalysts.
summary: Electrocatalysts are often assumed to be structurally stable; yet in practice, they continuously dissolve and restructure, directly affecting the number and nature of active sites and therefore performance. Although dissolution-redeposition-driven evolution is well recognized in some electrocatalysis communities, others still interpret activity and selectivity as properties of static surfaces. We argue that across electrocatalytic technologies, especially under demanding industrially relevant timescales, "static" electrocatalysts are a myth: even parts-per-billion metal fluxes can cumulatively change surface structure, poison membranes, degrade supports, and thus shift device performance. Controlling these changes requires a mechanistic understanding of when dissolution, transport, and redeposition are promoted or suppressed by, for instance, potential, pH, reactants, or local microenvironments. Here, we unify evidence for restructuring across metal and metal-derived catalysts under various electrochemical reactions, highlight common driving forces, and summarize the appropriate tools to quantify it. Ultimately, electrocatalysts should be evaluated, designed, and interpreted as dynamically stable materials and not as static electrochemical interfaces.

title: Exploratory comparative profiling of 22 macro- and trace elements reveals disrupted elemental homeostasis in colorectal cancer tissues.
summary: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is associated with systemic and local alterations in element homeostasis, yet tissue-level data remain limited and inconsistent. This study quantitatively profiled 22 macro- and trace elements in paired tumorous and histopathologically confirmed adjacent non-tumorous colonic tissues from 15 CRC patients using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). We observed significant accumulation of phosphorus (P), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg), iron (Fe), molybdenum (Mo), Rubidium (Rb), strontium (Sr), titanium (Ti), gallium (Ga), niobium (Nb), and zirconium (Zr) in tumor tissues, alongside a significant decrease in cobalt (Co). The intratumoral copper-to-zinc (Cu/Zn) ratio showed a nominal elevation that did not survive false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Critically, the strong positive correlations among macroelements (e.g., P, Ca, Mg) and essential trace elements in human body (e.g., Fe, Zn, Cu, Mo) consistently observed in adjacent non-tumorous tissues were substantially weakened or abolished in tumor tissues, suggesting a systemic collapse of coordinated elemental regulation within the tumor microenvironment. These findings indicate that tumor tissues exhibit accumulation of certain elements, which is associated with the elevated biosynthetic demands of proliferating cells, whereas the broader disruption of elemental networks is correlated with CRC pathogenesis. The widespread disturbance of trace element compositional homeostasis, rather than individual element alterations, may represent a more integrative biomarker for CRC diagnosis and progression.

title: Foam cell formation at the host-pathogen interface in tuberculosis and cryptococcosis
summary: Summary. Foam cells are lipid-laden macrophages that are associated with chronic inflammation in metabolic, infectious, and autoimmune diseases, plus with some cancers. Our previous work generated a shift from the atherogenesis paradigm in which foam cells are cholesterol-laden to a disease context paradigm in which the accumulated lipids can be various neutral lipids (triglycerides and/or cholesteryl esters). We also found that foam cell biogenesis may occur by different mechanisms even when the same neutral lipid species accumulates. In preliminary work, published and unpublished, we found that with two infectious pulmonary diseases, tuberculosis and cryptococcosis, infected macrophages accumulate triglycerides; however, with tuberculosis -- but not with cryptococcosis -- triglyceride accumulation is rapamycin-sensitive and TLR-2- dependent. Thus, as proposed in the present R21 application, comparative analysis of these two infections will identify shared as well as disease-specific mechanisms underlying neutral lipid accumulation in macrophages. To characterize the mechanisms of foam cell formation in tuberculosis and cryptococcosis, we propose to start with the host-pathogen interface. The R21 plan includes two specific aims. In the first aim, we will identify pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMP) triggering neutral lipid accumulation in infected macrophages by assessing the lipogenic effect on macrophages of purified and synthetic components as well as cell-wall- defective mutants of C. neoformans and M. tuberculosis. In the second aim, we will identify networks of macrophage pattern recognition receptors (PRR) implicated in C. neoformans- and M. tuberculosis-induced neutral lipid accumulation by assessing infection-induced lipid droplet accumulation in knock-down PRR macrophage mutants generated by CRISPRi technology. title: Host and bacterial factors mediate adverse pregnancy outcomes during perinatal listeriosis
summary: ABSTRACT Specialized pathogens that colonize gestational tissues during pregnancy are a major cause of morbidity and mortality. While these pathogens can induce devastating adverse pregnancy outcomes (APO) including spontaneous miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth (PTB), and invasive infant infections, little is known about the factors that permit successful gestational colonization or host pathways that mediate APO. TORCH pathogens are the most recognized among these; however, non-TORCH pathogens can also cause severe congenital infections. The gram-positive bacterial pathogen Listeria monocytogenes (Lm) causes the foodborne illness listeriosis. Although infection is mild and self-limiting in healthy adults, infection risk increases up to 18x during pregnancy and infant fatality rates can reach ~60%. Here, we propose to use Lm – a model bacterial pathogen – to dissect the host and bacterial factors that mediate gestational tissue colonization and onset of APO in a perinatal listeriosis mouse model. Recently, serotype 1/2a laboratory reference strains which are frequently used to probe Lm pathogenesis were shown to be genetically distinct from major serotype 4b human clinical isolates. The 4b clinical isolate 2203 caused strikingly high rates of maternal infection and APO (85 and 100% versus 13% and 25% annual averages). In this proposal, we will test the hypothesis that 2203: 1) induces an early and robust gestational inflammatory response causing high rates of APO, and 2) possesses novel genetic factors that confer its successful gestational replication. In preliminary infections, 2203 causes significantly increased colonization of the gravid uterus, pups, and placentas compared to 10403S. 2203 also induces significantly elevated APO, recapitulating PTB and stillbirth as observed in the human outbreak.
